answer:
What I ran: a 6-spin Heisenberg chain (J=1, spin = Pauli/2), started in up-down-up-down-up-down, evolved with a Trotter approximation (step 0.1, even and odd bonds alternating) to six times 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. All six circuits went in one job (ID 01a160a5-921d-7126-aea4-e54a443f295e) on garnet:mock with 1000 shots each. Each circuit measures all 6 spins. The server received 0, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 CZ gates for the six circuits. Mock jobs cost no credits.

What a perfect quantum computer shows (Neel order, 1 = perfect up-down pattern): 1.00 at t=0, 0.88 at 0.4, 0.62 at 0.8, 0.41 at 1.2, 0.34 at 1.6, 0.38 at 2.0. Those values come from noiseless simulation of the exact circuits I submitted. The exact solution of the model is almost the same (1.00, 0.8815, 0.6228, 0.4108, 0.3412, 0.3707), so the Trotter error is small. The order drops fast, falls to about a third by t of about 1.5, then levels off and starts to wobble, because 6 spins is a small system.

What the test device gave back: -0.24, -0.42, -0.40, -0.43, -0.40, -0.40. These do not track the physics. The mock returns random-looking results, not a simulation of my circuit. Every circuit, including t=0 where the right answer is exactly 1, came back as roughly equal counts of just four bitstrings (000000, 111111, and two alternating-pair patterns like 011011 or 100100), which is not what a real run would produce. So the mock only proves the job was accepted, compiled and returned in the right format. It says nothing about the spin chain, and the measured numbers should not be read as physics. A real-device run would be needed, and with 60 to 300 CZ gates the real hardware noise would likely wash out much of the later signal.

What this says about the real material: in a quantum antiferromagnet like KCuF3, the up-down order is not stable. Neighboring spins can flip-swap through the XX+YY terms, so starting from a perfect Neel pattern the order melts quickly (within about one to two time units of J) even at zero temperature. That is the quantum fluctuation effect: a 1D chain has no stable long-range Neel order, only short-range anti-alignment. A 6-site chain is a rough model, and the finite size causes the level-off and wobble.
